headline: Photos Replace Poaching: Indonesian Villages Turn Wildlife Into Income
meta_description: A pay-per-photo program across West Kalimantan has transformed 800+ villagers from hunters into conservationists, generating 378,000 wildlife observations.
summary_short: In Borneo, villagers now earn money photographing endangered orangutans and rare birds instead of hunting them—a shift that's reshaping forest protection.
body:
Across nine villages in West Kalimantan, Indonesia, more than 800 people have traded their hunting rifles for camera phones. Through KehatiKu, a conservation program funded through 2028, villagers earn supplemental income by photographing or recording wildlife—potentially earning up to $200 monthly for common species, with higher payouts for rare sightings. What began as a simple economic incentive has catalyzed a genuine shift in how local communities view their forests. A 72-year-old farmer named Imelda, who once hunted birds for their colorful plumage, now walks daily into the woods hoping to photograph an orangutan, the program's top prize. "We really, really want to protect them," she explains.

The numbers speak to the program's impact. Since its launch, participants have submitted 378,000 confirmed wildlife observations, including sightings of critically endangered species like the Bornean orangutan and Abbott's gibbon. That data has proven invaluable to scientists tracking population densities, animal ranges, and behavior patterns. Borneo Futures, the conservation consultancy running the initiative, funded its $300,000 launch through philanthropy—money directed toward a mobile app, artificial intelligence tools for species identification, and monthly payments to villagers.

What makes this strategy remarkable is its simplicity and human dimension. Octavius, a 50-year-old farmer, uses his earnings to pay for his children's college education. Another villager noted the mathematics: where hunting one bird once yielded 50,000 rupiah, a photograph now earns 5,000 to 10,000 rupiah with far less effort and no harm to the animal. As KehatiKu expands—two additional villages are joining next month—its managing director Erik Meijaard observes that "forests and wildlife is valued more for conservation than exploitation." In Borneo's intricate ecosystems, that revaluation may prove as precious as any photograph.
quick_facts: 800+ villagers across 9 West Kalimantan villages now photograph wildlife for income
Program generated 378,000 wildlife observations including critically endangered species
Villagers earn up to $200 monthly, with higher payments for rare species sightings
$300,000 philanthropic funding supports mobile app and monthly village payments through 2028
